title: A Factory Reuses Its Rinse Water
transcript:
At a small metalworking factory, the largest improvement in water use began with a question about a pipe. Clean water entered several rinsing tanks, but water leaving the final tank still contained far fewer impurities than water used at the beginning of the process. An engineer visiting the factory asked why every stage had to start with an entirely fresh supply.

The manager explained that the existing arrangement was simple to operate and had been in place for years. Changing it would require staff to monitor water quality more closely. Nevertheless, rising supply costs encouraged the factory to test a system that directed cleaner rinse water backwards to an earlier stage, where the quality requirements were less strict.

The trial was confined to one production line. Workers checked the finished parts as well as the water, because reducing consumption would have little value if more products needed to be processed again. Initial results showed lower water demand with no increase in rejected parts. However, a busy week revealed a problem: when several batches arrived close together, impurities accumulated faster than expected.

Instead of abandoning the trial, the team added a rule based on measured water quality rather than a fixed timetable. Water was replaced when readings reached a specified limit. Staff also received a clear procedure for switching back to the original arrangement if the monitoring equipment failed.

The factory is now considering whether the system suits its other lines. The manager stresses that the saving came from matching water quality to the task, not from assuming that all used water could circulate indefinitely. The next decision will depend on the cost of monitoring and the different materials handled elsewhere in the building.

questions.prompt: What opportunity did the visiting engineer notice?
options: Used water could be sold directly as drinking water.
Relatively clean water from a later stage might serve an earlier one.
The factory could stop checking the quality of finished parts.
Every rinsing tank contained exactly the same impurities.
questions.answer: Relatively clean water from a later stage might serve an earlier one.
questions.explanation: 最后一道清洗水较干净，可回用于质量要求较低的前段工序。

questions.prompt: Why were finished parts checked during the trial?
options: To make sure water savings did not cause more reprocessing or rejection.
To select a new colour for the factory’s products.
To determine how many workers preferred the old timetable.
To avoid measuring water quality altogether.
questions.answer: To make sure water savings did not cause more reprocessing or rejection.
questions.explanation: 若省水导致次品或返工增加，改造意义就会降低，因此同时检查成品。

questions.prompt: What problem appeared during a busy week?
options: No batches reached the trial production line.
Fresh water became colder than used water.
Impurities built up faster when batches arrived close together.
The factory discovered that every finished part had failed inspection.
questions.answer: Impurities built up faster when batches arrived close together.
questions.explanation: 批次密集时杂质积累比预计更快，固定换水节奏不适应生产波动。

questions.prompt: What determined when water was replaced under the revised procedure?
options: The manager’s arrival time each morning.
The number of visitors in the building.
A schedule that remained identical in every week.
Whether measured water quality reached a specified limit.
questions.answer: Whether measured water quality reached a specified limit.
questions.explanation: 修订后根据实际水质达到阈值换水，而非只依赖固定时间表。
